Kirjath-jearim
KUR-jath-JEE-uh-rim
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Qiryath Ye'arim (H7157), "city of forests" (from qiryah, "city," + ya'ar, "forest, wood"). A town in Judah, on the border of Benjamin, where the ark of the covenant rested for some twenty years.

📖 Biblical Definition

Kirjath-jearim ("city of forests") was a town in the territory of Judah where the ark of the covenant rested for about twenty years, between its return from the Philistines and its eventual removal to Jerusalem by David. After the Philistines captured the ark (1 Sam 4), the LORD afflicted them so grievously that they sent it back to Israel on a cart drawn by milk cows. It came to Beth-shemesh, where the LORD struck many men for irreverently looking into the ark; the frightened people of Beth-shemesh sent to the men of Kirjath-jearim, saying, "The Philistines have brought again the ark of the LORD; come ye down, and fetch it up to you" (1 Sam 6:21). So "the men of Kirjath-jearim came, and fetched up the ark of the LORD, and brought it into the house of Abinadab in the hill, and sanctified Eleazar his son to keep the ark of the LORD" (1 Sam 7:1). There the ark remained for some twenty years, through the latter days of Samuel and the reign of Saul, who never sought it (1 Chr 13:3). It was from Kirjath-jearim that David, having taken Jerusalem, sought to bring the ark up to the city — first by the cart, which ended in the death of Uzzah for steadying the ark irreverently (2 Sam 6:1-11), and then properly, borne by the Levites as the Law prescribed (1 Chr 15). Kirjath-jearim thus marks a strange and instructive interlude: for twenty years the ark, the symbol of God's presence and the throne of His glory, sat largely neglected in a private house on a hill, while Israel under Saul went about its affairs without seeking the LORD. It is a quiet picture of the danger of neglecting God's presence — of having the symbols of His glory among us yet leaving them unsought and unhonored — and a reminder, in David's eventual zeal to recover the ark, of the difference between a people that seeks the LORD and a people that ignores Him.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A town in Judah ("city of forests") where the ark of the covenant rested for some 20 years in the house of Abinadab, after its return from the Philistines and before David brought it to Jerusalem (1 Sam 7:1-2); a picture of God's presence neglected and then sought.

KIRJATH-JEARIM, proper noun. Hebrew Qiryath Ye'arim (H7157), "city of forests"; a town in Judah on the Benjamin border.

Where the ark of the covenant rested ~20 years after its return from the Philistines (1 Sam 7:1-2).

The men of Kirjath-jearim fetched the ark from Beth-shemesh and set it in the house of Abinadab, sanctifying Eleazar to keep it.

It remained there largely neglected through Samuel's later days and Saul's reign, who never sought it (1 Chr 13:3).

From there David brought it up to Jerusalem — first wrongly by cart (Uzzah's death, 2 Sam 6), then properly borne by the Levites (1 Chr 15).

📖 Key Scripture

1 Samuel 7:1-2 — "And the men of Kirjathjearim came, and fetched up the ark of the LORD, and brought it into the house of Abinadab in the hill, and sanctified Eleazar his son to keep the ark of the LORD. And it came to pass... that the time was long; for it was twenty years."

1 Chronicles 13:3 — "And let us bring again the ark of our God to us: for we enquired not at it in the days of Saul."

2 Samuel 6:6-7 — "And when they came to Nachon's threshingfloor, Uzzah put forth his hand to the ark of God, and took hold of it... And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah; and God smote him there for his error."

Psalm 132:6 — "Lo, we heard of it at Ephratah: we found it in the fields of the wood."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Kirjath-jearim is corrupted when the twenty-year neglect of the ark is overlooked, when the lesson about ignoring God's presence is missed, or when David's recovery of the ark is read apart from the reverence the LORD requires.

expand to see more

Neglect-of-presence missed. The most striking and sobering feature of the Kirjath-jearim interlude is the neglect: for some twenty years the ark of the covenant — the throne of God's glory, the symbol of His covenant presence with Israel — sat in a private house on a hill, while Israel under Saul went about its business without seeking it. As David later put it, "we enquired not at it in the days of Saul" (1 Chr 13:3). The picture is quietly devastating: the people of God had the symbols of His presence among them, yet left them unsought and unhonored. It is a warning to every generation that has the means of grace, the Word, the gathered church, the very presence of God in Christ — and yet neglects to seek Him. To possess the symbols of God's presence while ignoring Him is the spiritual state of Kirjath-jearim.

Kirjath-jearim has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the contrast between a people that neglects God's presence (Saul's Israel, leaving the ark unsought for twenty years) and a people that seeks Him (David's zeal to recover the ark). Yet even David had to learn that God's presence must be approached on His terms: his first attempt to bring up the ark by cart ended in Uzzah's death for irreverence (2 Sam 6:6-7), and only when the ark was borne by the Levites as the Law prescribed did the recovery succeed (1 Chr 15). The lesson is twofold: do not neglect God's presence, and do not presume to approach it carelessly. The God who must be sought must also be reverenced.
